extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of media studies/sociology (and journalists interested in theory of news production)
extracted.subtask_description: The page outlines the social processes and professional criteria by which media select, frame, transform and present events as 'news', including organisational constraints, news values, source relations, framing practices, and agenda-setting. Useful for analyzing how items become newsworthy and how media shape public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: A professional ideology of what constitutes 'good news' — an orientation to items which are 'out of the ordinary' but also includes items that concern elite persons or nations, are dramatic, can be personalised, have negative consequences, or fit existing newsworthy themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News values provide routine criteria enabling journalists and editors to decide which stories are 'newsworthy' and which are not. Events that score on multiple news values have greater news potential; items scoring high on all dimensions (e.g., Kennedy assassination: unexpected, dramatic, negative consequences, involved elite persons, part of recurrent theme) may trigger top-priority coverage (e.g., news-flash interruptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinariness / unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary or cardinal news value: orientation to items which are 'out of the ordinary' and breach normal expectations (e.g., sudden earthquake, moon-landing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists favour unusual/unexpected events because they represent changefulness and unpredictability; such items are more likely to be selected and played up by reporters to enhance newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliteness (concern with elite persons or nations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events involving elite persons or nations are more likely to be considered newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories about high-status individuals or powerful countries receive privileged coverage because institutional spokespeople and audiences assume such actors have greater relevance or impact; items involving elites can elevate an event's status and visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Events which are dramatic or can be presented dramatically increase news potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists will 'play up' dramatic elements in a story to enhance its newsworthiness; dramatic framing helps transform routine reports into headline material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalisation / human-interest appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that can be personalised to highlight human characteristics (humour, sadness, sentimentality) are attractive as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalisation connects abstract issues to individual stories, making them more comprehensible and emotionally resonant for audiences; papers differ in how much they prioritise human-interest (e.g., Daily Mirror).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity / consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Events with negative consequences are more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative or harmful outcomes (crime, disasters) attract media attention because they breach expectations of order and consensus and thus are 'problematic realities' requiring explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme membership / recurrent topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are part of, or can be made to appear part of, an existing newsworthy theme (e.g., hooliganism, crime waves, seasonal sports) are more likely to be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchorage in familiar topics increases the potential for translation into a public idiom and for linkage to prior coverage; recurrent themes help the media objectify issues and sustain agenda salience over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisational structuring of news (sections and staffing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine organisation of newspapers (home news, foreign, political, sport, specialist correspondents and departments) predisposes them to certain types of events and topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paper's structure (staffing, departments, institutional contacts) regularly directs selection toward categories it routinely covers; this produces distinct 'social personalities' of papers and influences what items are even considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/time/resource constraints (pre-scheduled events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incessant pressures of time and problems of resource allocation lead journalists to rely on pre-scheduled events and sources that regularly produce reportable activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covering pre-scheduled events reduces scheduling problems but increases dependence on sources willing/able to pre-schedule; this operational constraint shapes the agenda by privileging institutional actors who can reliably supply events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality, balance and objectivity as professional norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional rules distinguishing 'fact' and 'opinion' and seeking 'impartiality' and 'balance' guide reporting practices, especially in broadcast where regulation is stronger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These norms lead journalists to ground statements in 'objective' and 'authoritative' statements from 'accredited' sources, which both aim to preserve neutrality and orient reporting toward institutional definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accredited sources and the hierarchy of credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Media habitually turn to accredited representatives of institutions (MPs, ministers, employers, trade-union leaders, experts) whose authority confers 'objectivity' and 'authority' on their statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of time, impartiality requirements, and perceived authority, those in high-status institutional positions become primary definers; this structured over-accessing reproduces existing power structures in media representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary vs secondary definers (source-driven agenda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary definers (powerful institutional sources) establish the initial interpretation of a topic; media are usually secondary definers, reproducing or translating those definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A primary interpretation 'commands the field' and sets terms of reference for subsequent coverage; alternative voices must enter inside that interpretive framework, making fundamental challenge difficult (example: debates framed as 'numbers' constrain dissent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and contextualisation (making events intelligible)
rubrics_metrics.description: To present an event to an assumed audience the media must identify, name, relate it to other events, assign it a social context, and place it within cultural 'maps of meaning' so it 'makes sense'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing and contextualisation are essential journalistic practices that rely on shared cultural referents; without these cultural maps unusual events remain random and unintelligible to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity in reporting (selection and editing of statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The media do not reproduce all parts of a source's statement; they exercise selectivity and impose their own criteria on raw materials, choosing which statements or parts to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selectivity allows media to appropriate and transform institutional inputs; journalists choose elements that fit their paper's sense of newsworthiness and audience expectations, thereby shaping meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding into public idiom / mode of address
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paper develops a characteristic mode of address — its 'public idiom' — translating official viewpoints into a language form tailored to its target readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding determines rhetoric, imagery and assumed common stock of knowledge; translation into public idiom makes official definitions available and resonant to lay audiences and can naturalise dominant interpretations (example: Chief Inspector report turned into 'AGGRO BRITAIN' headline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation potential (newsworthiness + anchorage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a formal/expert statement can be transformed into a popular, dramatic form depends on its potential-for-translation (newsworthiness) and its anchorage in familiar long-standing topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all authoritative statements are equally 'translatable' into popular rhetoric; items anchored in familiar themes (e.g., hooliganism) are easier to dramatise and popularise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-setting and objectification of public concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrated media attention confers status of high public concern on highlighted issues; media set the public agenda by making issues appear objectively salient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media selection and translation can give issues more 'objective' status than technical reports alone; this agenda-setting function inserts everyday language back into the consensus and confirms issues as 'pressing' for public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial voice and mobilising the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond translation, the press may editorialise — using public idiom to express opinions, claim to 'speak the public voice', advocate lines of action, legitimize controllers, or mobilize public support for measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorialising is an active media role that can both reflect and shape assumed public opinion; editorials can serve to legitimate authority or to push for stronger measures by presenting views as if they represent majority sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduction vs transformation (media autonomy limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media reproduce dominant definitions due to structural imperatives but also perform transformative work in selecting, coding and dramatizing material; transformation is constrained by newsworthiness, organisational frameworks and ideological limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The media's creative role is not fully autonomous: transformations depend on the structured raw materials from primary definers and on institutional and professional constraints; still, selective transformation helps naturalise elite definitions within popular discourse.
